section_title: How is the accuser defeated, and why does his defeat bring a warning?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 Then a war broke out in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought back. 8 But the dragon was not strong enough, and no longer was any place found in heaven for him and his angels. 9 And the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world. He was hurled to the earth, and his angels with him.

10 And I heard a loud voice in heaven saying: “Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of His Christ. For the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down— he who accuses them day and night before our God. 11 They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they did not love their lives so as to shy away from death. 12 Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them! But woe to the earth and the sea; with great fury the devil has come down to you, knowing he has only a short time.”

context_lines: War breaks out in heaven. Michael and his angels fight the dragon and his angels, and the dragon loses. He and his angels are thrown down to the earth, with no place remaining for them in heaven. John explicitly names the defeated dragon as the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan.

A loud voice announces salvation, God’s kingdom and the authority of His Christ. It also explains one reason for heaven’s joy: the one who accused God’s people day and night has been thrown down. The battle concerns more than force; it includes accusations made against those who belong to God.

The victory of God’s people is attributed to the Lamb’s blood and to their faithful testimony. They remain faithful even when faced with death. In this vision, overcoming evil can include suffering martyrdom; victory is not defined simply as escaping harm.

Heaven is called to rejoice, but earth and sea receive a warning. The devil comes down in fury because he knows his time is short. His defeat is certain, yet his remaining activity brings danger to those he opposes.
common_interpretation_lines: Readings differ over when this heavenly conflict takes place. [Walvoord](https://swartzentrover.com/cotor/E-Books/holiness/Walvoord/Revelation/Rev_12.htm) expects a future expulsion connected with the great tribulation. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-revelation-of-jesus-christ/) relates the vision to the advance and trials of Christ’s kingdom in church history. Both take the ending of Satan’s role as accuser seriously, but place it within different timelines.

The [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/revelation/12) connect the serpent with Genesis and the expulsion with Jesus’ words about Satan falling from heaven. Such connections encourage readers to understand the scene alongside the wider biblical account of his defeat, rather than as an isolated description of heavenly warfare.

The passage itself states the foundation of the believers’ victory: the blood of the Lamb and their testimony, maintained even in the face of death. It does not give readers a new set of words for commanding angels or promise that faithful believers will never suffer.
god_plan_lines: In [John 12:31–33](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/12.htm), Jesus connects the judgment of the world’s ruler with His own coming death. Revelation likewise places the Lamb’s blood at the heart of victory over the accuser. This connection keeps attention on what Christ has accomplished while readers consider the vision’s disputed timing.

[Romans 8:33–39](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/8.htm) asks who can bring a charge against God’s people when God declares them righteous and Christ, who died and rose, speaks for them. It also names persecution and death without treating them as separation from His love. That gives fuller meaning to Revelation’s picture of overcoming: the enemy may bring suffering, but cannot overturn what God has done through Christ.
